translation: Two other small, scalloped-edge photos, likely from the same year, show the same child, but smaller now, in a dress with frills and balloon sleeves.
In the first, she is impishly snuggled against a woman with a large body encased in a wide-striped dress; her hair is wound up in large rolls.
In the second photo, she raises her left fist; her right is held back by a tall man's hand.
He is casually postured wearing a light-colored jacket and pleated pants.
Both photos were taken on the same day next to a low brick wall topped with flowers in its own paved courtyard.
Above their heads runs a clothesline where one pin has been forgotten.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but the paper of the booklet is more ordinary and the gold edging has disappeared—, likely destined for the same family distribution, shows a little girl of about four years old, serious, almost sad despite a chubby good-natured face under short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back with clips to which ribbons are attached, like butterflies.
Her left hand rests on the same intricately carved table, entirely visible in Louis XVI style.
She appears plump in her bodice; her suspender skirt hikes up at front because of a protruding belly—perhaps a sign of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment and they looked handsome in their uniforms.
On the evening of conscription, they toured the cafes to celebrate the glory of being recognized as real men.
Before joining the regiment, they were still kids and didn't have a worth in both job market and marriage.
Afterwards, they might have a wife and children.
The uniform that they showed off around town during leaves enveloped them in patriotic beauty and potential sacrifice.
The aura of victorious soldiers, of G. I. s, hovered around them.
The coarse fabric of their tunics, brushed when standing on tiptoe to embrace them, embodied an absolute divide between the world of men and that of women.
Seeing them evoked a sense of heroism.

Underneath the immutable, last year's circus posters featuring a photo of Roger Lanzac, first communion images distributed to companions, the Songwriters' Club on Radio Luxembourg, the days filled with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, people would cluster at the window of the general electronics store watching television.
Cafés invested in buying a set to attract customers.
Motocross tracks snaked up and down hillsides and we watched loud machines go up and down them all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce with its new catchwords "initiative", "dynamism" shook up small-town life.
Between fairground amusements and village festivals commercial markets established themselves as springtime rituals.
In downtown streets loudspeakers blared out invitations to buy punctuated by songs from Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine as prizes like cars or dining sets were offered to lucky winners.

On a podium in front of Town Hall an emcee told jokes just like Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard would have done it drew contestants for radio-style contests Quitte ou Double or catch-as-catch-can challenges while Commerce Queen sat pridefully at one corner wearing her crown under twinkling lights displayed her merchandise advancing under celebratory colors.
People remarked that "Business is sure changing" or "You've got not stay with it; if you stay home you'll never know what's going on".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be relived while eating and drinking.
They weren't skilled or convinced enough to talk about what they knew but hadn't seen.
Hence, no mentions of Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor of the starving who were gathered up each morning in the Warsaw Ghetto, nor of the 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Consequently, there was a feeling that history lessons, documentaries and films would later not dispel: neither the crematoriums nor the atomic bomb were situated in the same era as black market butter, air raid alerts and rushing to basements.
They were contrasting it with the previous war, the Great One, the war of '14, which was won in blood and glory, a real man's war that the women at the table listened to with respect.
They spoke of Chemin des Dames and Verdun, of gas victims, and of November 11th 1918 bells.
They named villages from which not a single child who went to fight had returned.
They opposed the soldiers in trench mud against 40's prisoners who stayed warm and sheltered for five years without even receiving bombs over their head.
Heroism and misfortune were subjects of their argument.

The children didn't listen and rushed to leave the table as soon as they received permission, taking advantage of the general benevolence on festive days to indulge in forbidden games, jumping on beds and swinging upside down.
Yet they retained everything.

Next to the fabulous times whose episodes they wouldn't order for a long time, the Debacle, Exodus, Occupation, Landing and Victory seemed dull compared with their nameless present where they grew up.
They regretted not having been born just yet when it was necessary to depart in cohorts along roads and sleep on straw like Bohemians.
Of this un-lived time they kept a tenacious regret.
Other's memories passed onto them a secret nostalgia for that era narrowly missed out on with prospects of experiencing it one day.
The frenzy that had followed the Liberation was fading.
People then only thought of going out, and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that constituted a first time since the war caused a rush; bananas, National Lottery tickets, fireworks.
Whole neighborhoods were flocking from circus fair to torchlight retreats; from grandma supported by her daughters to the baby in his pram.
They were pushed into Bouglione circus where they risked being trampled in the scramble.
As a concentrated and singing crowd, they would take to the road to welcome Our Lady of Boulogne's statue and walk her back for miles on end the next day.
Secular or religious gatherings, it didn't matter any opportunity was good if it meant being outside together as if they wanted to keep living collectively.

On Sunday evenings, buses would return from the sea with tall young men in shorts who sang at top volume looking out at beacon lights on luggage racks atop vehicles ahead or streetlights flying by overhead while dogs roamed freely and mated in plain view right on streets below.
Family story and social story are one and the same.

The voices of the dinner guests outlined the realms of their youth: the countryside and farms where, in times long past, men were farmhands and women were maids; the factory where they all met, got to know each other and married, as well as small businesses that ambitious ones aspired to start.
Their stories depicted lives devoid of personal events other than births, weddings and funerals.
Lives marked by hard work's toll on their bodies, threatened by alcoholism; devoid of voyages beyond a distant garrison town for their military service.
School was nothing more than a mythic backdrop a brief golden age presided over by a harsh god in the form of an instructor wielding an iron ruler used to rap knuckles.
The browned photographs on stained backs passed from hand to hand all the hands that had held them in other meals, a mix of coffee and grease blended into an indefinable color.
In the stiff and serious newlyweds, the wedding guests arranged in several rows along a wall, no one recognized their relatives or anyone else.
It wasn't oneself seen in the half-naked baby of indistinct gender on a cushion either, but someone else a creature belonging to a time that was silent and unreachable.
